newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Bougainville peace talks to resume under NZ wing.
newsitem.headline: Bougainville peace talks to resume under NZ wing.

text.p: Peace talks aimed at ending nine years of secessionist war on Papua New Guinea's Bougainville Island will begin this weekend in New Zealand, Foreign Minister Don McKinnon said on Wednesday.
Efforts to restart talks in a neutral country had begun in February, McKinnon said, but had been held up by a political crisis in Papua New Guinea (PNG) spurred by the Sandline mercenary affair.

The meeting, at an army camp, is due to bring together senior members of the PNG-backed Bougainville transitional government, the Bougainville interim government and its military wing, the Bougainville Revolutionary Army (BRA), he added.

"This is a step along the path towards settlement of their differences with the Papua New Guinea government. It should not be assumed there is a quick-fix solution to the situation in Bougainville," McKinnon told reporters.

He noted that initially the only parties due at the talks at Burnham army camp, near the South Island city of Christchurch, would be representatives of Bougainvillean groups, and would number 40 to 60 people.
"It is the expressed wish of the Bougainvilleans to gather for private discussions on how to bring about peace and reconstruction," the minister told a news conference.
"New Zealand is not a party to the Bougainville dispute and we will not participate in the talks themselves," he said, adding the hosts saw their role as providing logistical support.
Those attending include five MPs in the national PNG parliament who represent the island.
The conflict on the resource-rich island, 800 kilometres (500 miles) northeast of Port Moresby, has claimed thousands of lives and dates back to 1988.

Its main focus has been the Panguna copper mine in the island's central mountains, owned by a unit of Anglo-Australian mining giant Rio Tinto, which was closed by PNG Defence Forces (PNGDF) after clashes in 1989 and a state of emergency declared.
A series of peace talks backed by New Zealand and Australia started in 1990, and the most recent round took place in Cairns in Australia in late 1995.

When that ended the parties pledged to continue discussions. In March this year, PNG was plunged into its worst crisis since independence in 1975 when the army revolted against a government plan to use mercenaries from Anglo-South African company Sandline to end the Bougainville revolt.

Prime Minister Sir Julius Chan, who championed the US$36 million mercenary contract, lost his seat in national elections on Tuesday, and said his career in politics had been brought to an end by the affair.
McKinnon told Reuters New Zealand's offer to reopen the talks followed discussions with "all the key players in the region", including the PNG and Australian governments.

"All of them are very supportive of what we are doing and do hope to see some success come out of it. There is obviously uncertainty over what will (emerge), but all believe it is very timely and do wish to see it proceed," he said.
Despite the Sandline incident, which had "stalled" efforts for a while, McKinnon said he had been actively seeking to get the talks back on track since February.
Answering questions in parliament later in the day, the minister said he thought it might take a couple of months or longer for PNG to get a new government after Chan's defeat.
McKinnon's initiative, which came as a surprise to most observers here, won cross-party support in the chamber, with opposition MPs noting New Zealand's impartiality in the region.

The New Zealand Airforce will be responsible for bringing the meeting's participants to New Zealand at the end of this week, with aircraft calling at Port Moresby, the Solomon Islands, Bougainville itself and its offshore island of Buka.
